video_title: Rich Friedman on the Rise of Private Markets and AI Investing
gist: Rich Friedman, chairman of Goldman Sachs Asset Management and founder of its Principal Investment Area, argues private equity's binding constraint today is exits rather than operating performance, with thousands of firms and $3-5 trillion of unsold portfolio inventory and neither public markets nor strategics able to absorb it. He describes a deliberately capped deal cadence (five to seven investments a year), partial 'tempered' participation in manias including today's AI push, and a franchise built by adding credit, real estate, infrastructure and Asia only when GSAM could responsibly deploy the capital. Note: the available captions stop around the 29-minute mark, just as the host pivots to what excites him today, so the episode's AI-investing segment is not covered by this transcript.

insights.claim: Private equity's problem today is exits, not operating performance: Rich Friedman says portfolio company operating performance is about as good as it can be across the whole portfolio while the ability to sell has slowed sharply.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Diligence on sponsors should focus on realization/DPI and exit pipelines rather than EBITDA growth; secondaries, continuation vehicles and NAV finance are the pressure valves.
insights.quote: The crisis today in the PE industry ... is exits. It's not operating performance. ... Everything's slowed. Let's put it that way.

insights.claim: Friedman does not expect public markets or strategic acquirers to buy the bulk of private equity's existing portfolio inventory, and points instead to 'industrial transactions with PE firms together' - sponsor-to-sponsor combinations - as a likely clearing mechanism.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Implies continued heavy sponsor-to-sponsor deal flow and PE-firm consolidation rather than an IPO-led reopening; positive for advisory fees on sponsor-to-sponsor M&A, negative for near-term LP distributions.
insights.quote: the public market and the strategic ... market aren't going to be big buyers of the ... lion's share of the inventory, if you will.

insights.claim: Friedman sizes the private equity industry's unsold inventory at three to five trillion dollars of assets 'needing to find a home' across an industry with thousands of competing firms.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A concrete scale for the exit overhang; anything that unclogs it (rate cuts, IPO window, secondaries capital) is a multi-trillion-dollar release valve, and until then LP liquidity stays constrained.
insights.quote: an industry with thousands of competitors, three ... to five trillion of assets in inventory needing ... to find a home. I would have never imagined.

insights.claim: The host notes the private equity slowdown is already visible in year-over-year M&A statistics, where corporate and tech deal activity is diverging from sponsor activity.
insights.speaker: host, Alison
insights.so_what: Corporate/strategic M&A recovering while sponsor M&A lags is a tradeable divergence for advisory-revenue exposure and for sponsor-heavy credit books.

insights.claim: Although the PE industry now has thousands of firms, Friedman says only two to four of them meaningfully engage on any given business for sale, because the volume of activity means no firm can look at everything.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Cuts against the assumption that record dry powder automatically means auction-level entry multiples; disciplined mid-market buyers can still transact at non-momentum prices.
insights.quote: two to three or four that really pay attention and ... get involved. And that's because there's so much ... activity that you can't look at everything.

insights.claim: Deal-by-deal diligence costs of roughly $2 million are what thin out bidder lists: Friedman says the couple of mid-sized deals GSAM signed in the prior week drew only one or two other competitors rather than the ten or twenty of past cycles.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Rising process costs are an effective barrier to entry that favors large, repeat sponsors with relationship-sourced deals over broad-auction participants.
insights.quote: no one wants to be in ... something where you have to pay for due diligence ... and spend $2 million against 10 other people.

insights.claim: Friedman's framework for competition is that the number of rivals barely matters because a single other credible bidder is enough to make a process fully competitive on price.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Suggests entry multiples are set by the marginal bidder, not by aggregate dry powder - so counting industry AUM is a poor predictor of deal pricing.
insights.quote: it really only takes one other, you know, ... party to create a very competitive circumstance.

insights.claim: GSAM's private equity business has deliberately targeted only five to seven investments a year since roughly 2005-2006 and still runs at that cadence, invoking Warren Buffett's punch-card idea that you get a limited number of punches on your ticket.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A capped deal count is a usable filter for evaluating managers: strategies whose deal counts scale with fund size are implicitly loosening selection standards.
insights.quote: We can have a great business with five to ... seven decent-sized investments a year.

insights.claim: Friedman says the pressure to be active in AI today is the same pressure he faced in the late 1990s over AOL and Netscape, and that chasing momentum has historically not worked for his teams because 'those things crash.'
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A senior allocator explicitly framing the AI investment rush as a momentum period comparable to 1999 - a caution flag for late-cycle private AI valuations.
insights.quote: you're not active in AI right now, you know, ... you're useless.

insights.claim: Friedman's practical answer to mania pressure is 'tempering': in the 2000-era fund about $500-600 million, or roughly 10% of the fund, went into tech and telecom, which faded away without killing the fund while letting the franchise say it was playing.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A sizing rule for hot themes - cap the thematic sleeve near 10% of the vehicle so a blow-up is survivable; applicable to how LPs should judge managers' AI exposure today.
insights.quote: about $500 or $600 million of that fund sort ... of got invested in tech and telecom. And then-- ... but that was 10%.

insights.claim: Friedman says the pace of adding new fund strategies was gated by whether capital could be responsibly deployed, not by whether it could be raised - which slowed the build but left the firm first-mover in several product lines.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: The inverse test for today's alternatives managers, whose product proliferation is often fundraising-led; deployment capacity, not AUM growth, is the quality signal.
insights.quote: [It] wasn't a matter of, could we raise the money? ... It's could we responsibly invest the money?

insights.claim: Goldman's private credit business began as a late-1990s subordinated debt fund created because Europe had no private subordinated debt market for buyouts, and the fund ended up competing directly with the US public high yield market for deals.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Private credit's origin as a fill-in for absent public markets frames today's question of how much of it is genuine market-gap lending versus public-market substitution.

insights.claim: Friedman says the post-crisis senior debt fund generated equity-like returns despite lending at LIBOR plus roughly 250 basis points plus fees, a result he found surprising enough that he never imagined running senior debt inside a merchant bank.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Dislocation-era senior secured paper produced equity returns off modest coupons - the template for why credit-dislocation dry powder is valuable when the current exit logjam forces sales.
insights.quote: Tom Connolly was running it. We made ... equity-like returns in that senior debt vehicle

insights.claim: Goldman's entry into tech and growth investing was pushed on a resistant team by the Executive Office around 2000 and funded off balance sheet and with employee money in $3-6-9 million option-sized bets, which is how the firm came to own 13% of Alibaba at its formation after having owned 10% of Qualcomm a decade earlier.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Small option-sized positions in an unfamiliar area, not conviction sizing, produced the franchise's largest outcomes - an argument for deliberate small-bet exposure to areas outside core competence.
insights.quote: we didn't know that looking back in time, ... that we could, at one point, own 13% of Alibaba ... when it was being formed.

insights.claim: Friedman describes the 2005-2007 buyout boom as the only time in history the public markets invited private equity to take them private, with roughly $200 billion of buyouts done in an 18-month period at valuations he says were not that crazy.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A marker for what a genuine take-private wave looks like in volume and in the direction of demand, useful for judging whether current public-to-private activity is comparable.
insights.quote: it was the first time in history ... where the public markets were saying, ... "We want you, private equity, to buy us."

insights.claim: Running principal investing inside a bank was, in Friedman's words, a fragile business model that was not central to the firm's advisory and trading businesses, required protection from the Executive Office to survive, and forced the strategy to partner with rather than compete against the firm's private equity and corporate clients instead of bidding in every auction.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: The channel-conflict tax on bank-affiliated sponsors is real and shrinks their opportunity set versus independent firms - a structural handicap to price when banks build or shed principal-investing arms.
insights.quote: it was a fragile business model for the firm

insights.claim: Friedman refuses to approve deals that pass on a 60/40 or 55/45 head count, requiring strong consensus from the investment committee before capital is committed.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A consensus threshold is a concrete governance test to ask managers about; split-vote approvals are where process risk concentrates.
insights.quote: we'd never approve ... deals if it was like 60/40 or 55/45 if ... you counted heads. We wanted a strong consensus ... of support for any investment that we made.

insights.claim: Friedman justifies consensus-based decision making on the grounds that investing is prediction and, in his words, humans are not very good at it - so the process, not the chairman's judgment, has to carry the weight.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Epistemic humility as an operating rule; a manager whose returns trace to one person's calls carries key-man and overconfidence risk.
insights.quote: as smart as we are, you know, ... this is predicting the future. It's like, we're ... not so good at this.

insights.claim: Friedman's committee rule is that forceful disagreement is encouraged from even the most junior partners but antagonism is not, because hostile behavior spirals and suppresses the input the process depends on.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Separating dissent from hostility is the mechanism that keeps a committee from becoming a rubber stamp - a cultural detail to probe in manager diligence.
insights.quote: it's okay to disagree. You ... can disagree. And you can disagree with force.

insights.claim: Friedman holds that returns are the precondition for everything else in an asset management business and that large amounts of employee capital invested alongside clients is what keeps the wider firm invested in those returns.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: GP and employee commitment levels are the alignment metric he treats as load-bearing - worth checking as a percentage of fund size when allocating.
insights.quote: You don't have good returns. Forget it.

insights.claim: Goldman's edge in China came from arriving before competitors with a small team and no local knowledge, then staffing with Western-trained Chinese nationals based in Hong Kong and Shanghai rather than expatriates.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Local-national staffing plus first-mover timing is the repeatable pattern behind emerging-market franchise value, and the model to test against newer entrants in India or the Gulf.
insights.quote: we had nationals who were ... Western trained, and we felt also had the DNA of a ... Goldman Sachs person

insights.claim: The ICBC investment - made by both the firm and its funds alongside a commercial relationship - was the seminal deal that established Goldman as a constructive investor in China, and Friedman says no other US bank had the opportunity to participate in that privatization.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Shows how a single strategic anchor investment can buy decades of market access - the access, not the deal economics, was the durable asset.

insights.claim: Friedman's model of deal origination is compounding rather than linear - one completed deal generates roughly three more - which is why he insisted on a trusted, long-tenured local leader in Asia rather than remote oversight from New York.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: Deal-flow compounding means early regional presence has convex value, and manager continuity in a region is a proxy for sourcing quality.
insights.quote: The deal industry has always been like one deal ... leads to three others.

insights.claim: Friedman says the consensus during the global financial crisis - that a wall of debt financings would fail to refinance and every private equity investment would go under - simply did not happen.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A direct precedent for discounting maturity-wall panics; refinancing walls have historically been renegotiated rather than realized as mass default.
insights.quote: there was just a wall of debt financings ... that-- it wasn't going to happen. And every ... private equity investment was going to fail.

insights.claim: Friedman's recency-bias check, borrowed from a colleague he calls Lloyd, is that today's crisis always feels worse than the last one only because the last one is over - the frame he applies to the current private-markets exit freeze.
insights.speaker: Rich Friedman
insights.so_what: A discipline check when weighing today's private-market stress against historical drawdowns before repricing the asset class.
insights.quote: today's crisis is worse ... than that crisis because that crisis is over.
